tier_reason: First-party ops/sec tables against LevelDB, RocksDB and Kyoto Cabinet (via JNI, default parameters). The benchmark code is public (count-db-run/src/main/java/be/bagofwords/db/benchmarks/bigrams/BigramTestsMain.java and uniform/UniformDataTestsMain.java) and the CPU is stated (i7-4770), but the JVM version and flags are not. Ratios reach ~95x with flags unstated, so the >50x rule also caps it at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Bigram-count test, 8 threads, ops/sec. Writing 256M counts: count-db 1.12E7 vs LevelDB 1.37E5 (~82x, derived from page data; the README rounds this to '80 times') and RocksDB 1.40E5. Reading 256M counts: 1.06E7 vs LevelDB 8.90E5 (~12x, derived from page data; the README says '11 times') and RocksDB 4.93E5. Across 1M-256M items, count-db beats LevelDB by ~19x-82x on writes and ~3.9x-15x on reads (derived from page data). Uniform-count test at 128M: write 1.48E7 vs LevelDB 1.56E5 (~95x, derived), RocksDB 1.07E5 and Kyoto Cabinet 2.01E6; read 2.29E7 vs LevelDB 8.32E5 (~28x, derived). In the mixed parallel test at 128M: read 1.75E6 and write 1.74E6, vs LevelDB 2.02E5 and 1.24E5.
corrections.caveats: Old (2015-era) hardware: an i7-4770 with a 7200rpm SATA HDD, no SSD. JVM version and flags are unstated. First-party benchmark. All baselines run with default parameters through JNI bindings. In the benchmark source, count-db runs with its in-process CACHED_AND_BLOOM caching layer while the (now commented-out) baseline lines use DatabaseCachingType.DIRECT. The LevelDB adapter implements each count increment as a get-then-put read-modify-write, with no merge operator. The workload therefore favours count-db's write-combining counter design over general-purpose stores. Ratios reach ~95x (uniform write vs LevelDB), above the >50x implausibility threshold with flags unstated, which caps it at tier C. The benchmark-source links in doc/performance.md are dead because the code moved to count-db-run/.

notes: Every raw number in the record matches doc/performance.md. The ~80x and ~11x figures come from the README; the page itself has only raw tables, so ratios are now marked as derived. Metadata checks out: MIT, 57 stars, not a fork or archived, last commit 2019-10-31, abandoned. The main shortcoming is the asymmetric setup: a cached, write-combining count-db against uncached read-modify-write LevelDB and RocksDB adapters.

tier_reason: First-party charts against RocksDB (rocksdbjni 5.7.2, tuned options, WAL disabled) and KyotoCabinet. The benchmark code is public (benchmarks/src/main/java/com/oath/halodb/benchmarks/BenchmarkTool.java, RocksDBStorageEngine.java) and the CPU and SSD are stated, but the JVM version and flags are not, so this is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The charts on the page are value-labelled. On 500M records, 8-byte keys and 1024-byte values: fill-random 127 MB/s vs RocksDB 10 and KyotoCabinet 14 (~12.7x vs RocksDB, derived from page data); random update 19 MB/s vs RocksDB 2 and KyotoCabinet 4 (~9.5x, derived); random read with 32 threads 94,409 ops/s vs RocksDB 59,936 and KyotoCabinet 86,230 (~1.6x, derived); mixed read+update 45,750 reads/s and 6,144 writes/s vs RocksDB 8,625 and 2,691 (~5.3x and ~2.3x, derived). HaloDB LOSES the fill-sequential test to RocksDB: 133 MB/s vs 165 MB/s (~0.81x), though it beats KyotoCabinet's 31.
corrections.caveats: The author states HaloDB is not always better than RocksDB, and supports only a subset of RocksDB's features (no range scans), so the comparison 'is not exactly fair to RocksDB'. RocksDB beats HaloDB on sequential fill. HaloDB keeps all keys and metadata in an in-memory index, so it uses more RAM and disk space and has a slow index rebuild on startup. The baseline is old: rocksdbjni 5.7.2 (2017), with the WAL disabled and Snappy compression in the bench config. JVM version and flags are unstated. First-party benchmark, run on RHEL 6 / kernel 2.6.32.

notes: Downgraded because the claim was overstated: RocksDB wins the fill-sequential test (165 vs 133 MB/s), so HaloDB does not win 'across fill/read/update tests'. The record gave no numbers and said the page has none, but every embedded chart is value-labelled, so claimed_speedup now carries the chart values (numbers_found_on_page is null because there were no record numbers to check). Metadata checks out: Apache-2.0, 528 stars, not archived or a fork, last commit 2023-04-26, abandoned.

tier_reason: First-party README table against BoltDB (bbolt v1.4.3) and BadgerDB (v4.9.1). The benchmark code is public (bench/compare/compare.go), but the CPU model is unstated ('Linux, 4 CPU'), the Go toolchain is given only by go.mod's 'go 1.25.4', and the durability mode behind the table is unspecified, so this is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: It wins only on random writes: 1.19M/s vs BoltDB's 0.23M/s (README: '5x faster'; ~5.2x derived from page data). It is slower than BoltDB on the other three columns: sequential write 1.98M/s vs 2.77M/s, read 0.44M/s vs 1.17M/s, and miss-read 1.08M/s vs 1.96M/s. BadgerDB beats it on every column: 7.30M/6.97M/1.29M/1.49M per second, i.e. ~3.7x on sequential writes and ~5.9x on random writes (derived from page data; the README says '4x behind').
corrections.caveats: The only win is random writes vs BoltDB (a B+tree, where random inserts are its known weak case). It is slower than BoltDB on sequential writes, reads and miss-reads, and slower than BadgerDB everywhere. CPU model unstated; Go toolchain only implied by go.mod (go 1.25.4). bench/compare runs several durability modes (NoWAL, SyncAsync, SyncAlways vs BoltDB/BadgerDB with and without sync), and the README does not say which mode the table shows. The license is declared only by a one-word 'License: MIT' README section: there is no LICENSE file or copyright notice, and GitHub reports none, so confirm with the author before vendoring. BoltDB is not one of the category's named incumbents, though it is a widely used embedded KV store (bbolt/etcd). 2 stars; single-writer toy engine.

notes: Downgraded because the claim was overstated by omission: the README table shows lsm-tree-go losing to BoltDB on 3 of 4 columns, which the record never said. The README explicitly declares MIT, so license and usability are corrected to MIT/copyable, with a caveat that there is no LICENSE file. Other metadata checks out: 2 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-05-31, active.
